name: PT Elang Mahkota Teknologi Tbk

frontmatter.title: Elang Mahkota Teknologi — a conglomerate priced as an option
frontmatter.summary: EMTK trades below the book value of the parent's equity while its operating businesses — free-to-air television, BUKA and Vidio, a hospital network and aviation ground services — still earn a positive operating profit and the group holds more cash than debt. We initiate at Buy: the DCF values the group well above the market price on a bridge that credits the reported net cash and the investment balance, with no deduction for Superbank because the bank is an associate, not a consolidated subsidiary.
thesis: EMTK's market capitalisation is below the parent's share of book equity even though the group still earns a positive operating profit and holds more cash than interest-bearing debt; the discount is a holding-company discount, not an operating loss.

FY2025 reported profit was flattered by one-off gains on taking control of BUKA and on the listed investment portfolio; we exclude them, and we book the foreign-exchange gain as non-operating income rather than as a recurring operating credit.
Free-to-air television is in structural decline, but the media segment still earns the largest segment result and funds the digital, healthcare and aviation-support build-out.

The decisive swing factors are the size of the truly distributable cash — the group publishes no parent-level total — and whether BUKA stops consuming capital. Superbank's balance sheet is not inside the group's — it is an associate whose deposits never reach the consolidated liabilities.
Catalysts are quarterly segment disclosure, portfolio simplification (the Indopay divestment is the latest step) and any narrowing of the holding-company discount.

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Elang Mahkota Teknologi (EMTK) with a **BUY** rating and a target price of Rp485, implying 65.5% from the last close. EMTK is not a single business: it is a holding company that controls a free-to-air television broadcaster, a digital marketplace and streaming platform, a private hospital network, an aviation ground-services operator and a small listed bank, and it carries a portfolio of listed minority stakes on top [S3].

The market is not pricing those parts as a going concern. At the last close the whole group is capitalised below the book value attributable to the parent's own shareholders, even though consolidated revenue in the last fiscal year was IDR19,120.0bn and the group reported a positive operating profit of IDR1,206.0bn [S3]. The gap is a holding-company discount: investors do not believe the cash on the consolidated balance sheet can be extracted, and they do not believe the television cash flow will last.

Our answer is that both doubts are partly right and both are overpriced. The base case below gives EMTK no credit for the revaluation gains that made FY2025 look spectacular; it models the operating businesses and the interest income on the cash book at the yield the 2026 quarters actually earn, and it charges the minorities their share. On that basis the discounted cash flow produces an equity value of Rp386 per share, on a bridge that adds the net cash, deducts the minority interest and adds the listed investment portfolio. The target of Rp485 is not that number rolled forward: it is the blend of the DCF (70.0% weight) with an EV/Sales cross-check (30.0%) that lands above the DCF, rolled at the cost of equity and weighted across the three scenarios. The DCF on its own would support a materially lower figure, and we say so rather than present the blend as the DCF. The drivers that produce our return, in order of size, are: (i) the cash and investment bridge against the minority claim, taken from the 30 September 2026 balance sheet [S0]; (ii) the DCF operating value on a revenue base of IDR19,120.0bn that includes a full year of BUKA, growing at the pace the nine months already booked imply [S0, S3]; and (iii) the EV/Sales weight and the bull probability, which together account for the gap between the DCF and the target and are argued in the valuation section.

What moves the value, in order: the treatment of the cash bridge; the durability of the media segment result; and the minority share of profit, which is large because every operating subsidiary has outside holders [S3]. The rating is BUY, and the single question that produced the round-one HOLD was the bank. Superbank is a listed associate, not a consolidated subsidiary: EMTEK holds it through PT Elang Media Visitama alongside Grab, Singtel and KakaoBank [S3 p.35], and the FY2025 consolidated balance sheet reports total liabilities of IDR7,379.0bn against the bank's own customer deposits of IDR17,600.0bn at 30 September 2026 [S3, S8]. If the bank were inside the consolidation, its deposits alone would more than double group liabilities. Neither its assets nor its deposits are in the group's balance sheet, so no deduction from group cash is due and none is made; the stake is carried inside the investment balance the bridge already counts once. The bank is small in earnings but not in balance sheet: total assets of IDR27,500.0bn, loans of IDR13,800.0bn and pre-tax profit of IDR385.1bn for the nine months to September [S8, S7].

Indonesian media conglomerates have historically traded at a discount to the sum of their listed parts because
control sits with a founding family and because the listed subsidiaries are themselves thinly traded. The discount
narrows when a group sells assets and returns cash, and widens when a group raises equity in subsidiaries whose
proceeds stay inside the group.

EMTK is a Jakarta-based holding company founded in 1983 and listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange. It reports five operating segments: Media; Digital Products and Services; Healthcare; Aviation Support Services; and Others, which bundles technology, digital infrastructure and financial services [S3]. Consolidated revenue in FY2025 was IDR19,120.0bn, up from IDR12,233.0bn the year before, but the increase is mostly a scope change rather than organic growth: BUKA became a subsidiary during the year after PT Kreatif Media Karya purchased an additional 9.4% of BUKA's shares, taking the group over the control threshold and forcing full consolidation [S3].

**Media.** The media arm operates through PT Surya Citra Media, which owns the SCTV and Indosiar free-to-air networks and a portfolio of digital content properties, with MOJI and Mentari TV alongside them. The group reports a total free-to-air audience share of 38.1% across its four television networks at the end of 2025 [S3], the strongest single asset in the portfolio and the reason the segment still produces the largest segment result in the group [S3]. Media revenue is advertising revenue: it moves with national advertising spend, with programming ratings, and with the migration of advertising budgets to digital platforms. Program content is the dominant cost and is expensed as incurred, so the segment's margin is a function of content discipline as much as of the advertising cycle [S3].

**Digital Products and Services.** This segment contains BUKA, the marketplace, and Vidio, the streaming platform, with the group's digital advertising and content properties. It is the growth engine and the loss engine at once. BUKA's revenue grew 46.0% in FY2025 and its EBITDA improved after cost and portfolio restructuring [S3], but the group also reports that digital profitability moderated during the year [S3]. Vidio is described as Indonesia's largest over-the-top platform, monetised through subscriptions, advertising tiering, sports rights and, more recently, virtual gifting [S3].

**Healthcare.** The healthcare segment operates through PT Sarana Meditama Metropolitan, which runs the EMC Healthcare hospital network in Jakarta, Tangerang, Bekasi and Bogor and which acquired Kedoya Adyaraya and invested in Jakarta Eye Center in earlier years [S3]. Revenue is fee-for-service with a mix of inpatient, outpatient and diagnostic work; it grows with capacity, insurance penetration and a case mix shifting towards higher-value procedures [S3].

**Aviation Support Services.** Through PT Cahaya Aero Services (formerly Cardig Aero Services), acquired a majority stake in 2024, the group provides ground handling, cargo handling, aircraft release and maintenance, catering and aviation training, supporting more than 80,000 aircraft movements in 2025 [S3]. This is a contract business tied to airport traffic and airline customers, with a lower margin than media but longer revenue visibility.

**Others and the bank.** The residual segment contains connectivity, technology services and financial services. PT Superbank Indonesia, formerly Bank Fama, is an associate held through PT Elang Media Visitama, with Grab, Singtel and KakaoBank as co-shareholders [S3 p.35]; it completed an initial public offering in December 2025 that raised IDR2,790.0bn in gross proceeds and listed the bank separately [S3]. The IPO matters twice over: it validates a valuation for the digital bank, and it puts a public price on a stake that sits inside the group's investment balance rather than inside its consolidation [S3].

**Group structure and control.** The group is controlled by the Sariaatmadja family; the exchange register shows a free float of 22.4%, so the remainder is held by the family and affiliated holding entities [S0]. Control runs through a chain of holding entities, and the consolidated subsidiaries (SCMA, BUKA, SAME, CASS) each have their own outside shareholders [S3]. The consequence for an EMTK shareholder is that a large part of group operating profit is not attributable to them, which the model reflects through the minority assumption [S3].

**Recent portfolio action.** On 2 November 2026 the company sold virtually all of PT Indopay Merchant Services, the merchant-acquiring business, and deconsolidated it [S2]. The stated effect is that Indopay's financial statements are no longer consolidated [S2]. This fits a pattern of tidying the portfolio around the media, digital, healthcare and aviation core, and it removes a payments business whose economics were tied to merchant discount rates rather than to content and healthcare.
EMTK sits across four industries that behave very differently, and the report is clearer if they are treated separately [S3].

**Free-to-air television.** Indonesian FTA television is a mature, advertising-funded oligopoly. The regulator, the Indonesian Broadcasting Commission, has publicly warned that digital advertising spending is pressing on the television and radio industry and has called for collaboration among broadcasters to meet the digital challenge [S5]. That is the structural story in one sentence: the advertising pool is shifting to platforms the broadcasters do not own, and the broadcasters' response is to defend audience share and build or buy digital distribution. EMTK's answer has been to keep its four networks at a combined 38.1% audience share [S3] while pushing its own digital properties, so that demand leaving linear television can be at least partly recaptured inside the group.

The moat here is distribution density and content rights rather than technology: four national networks with established news, drama and sports franchises, plus long-standing advertiser relationships. An audience share of 38.1% is evidence the moat holds at the viewer level [S3]. The weakness is pricing power: rates are negotiated annually against audience delivery, and a shrinking pool means the segment can defend share and still lose revenue, which is what its revenue did between FY2024 and FY2025 [S3].

**Digital platforms.** The Indonesian marketplace and streaming market is a scale game with well-capitalised competitors and thin unit economics. BUKA's 46.0% revenue growth in FY2025 and improved EBITDA after restructuring [S3] show the business can grow into its cost base, but the group also acknowledges that digital profitability moderated [S3]. Streaming is a content-cost treadmill: sports rights and original series are the price of subscription growth, and Vidio's expansion into Malaysia [S3] spreads content cost over a larger subscriber base. The question for a value investor is not whether digital grows but whether it earns above the cost of capital; on the group's own disclosure it does not yet [S3].

**Healthcare.** Private hospital demand in Indonesia grows with insurance coverage, urbanisation and the shift of higher-income patients away from public provision. Capacity, doctor recruitment and case mix are the constraints, and the group's own commentary is about advancing into higher-value medical services and operational excellence rather than about price [S3]. This is the segment with the most durable growth and the least cyclicality in the portfolio.

**Aviation support.** Ground and cargo handling are contract businesses tied to airport throughput and airline customers, with high operating leverage and modest capital intensity. The disclosure of more than 80,000 aircraft movements supported in 2025 [S3] frames the scale. Competition is by tender and service quality; the moat is the incumbency of handling licences at specific airports.

**Five-forces view.** For media, buyer power is high (advertisers concentrate budgets and can move to digital), substitute pressure is high and rising, supplier power is moderate (talent and content), new entry is effectively blocked by spectrum and licensing, and rivalry is concentrated among a few national networks. For healthcare, buyer power is moderate and rising with insurers, supplier power is high for specialists, entry is capital-intensive but not blocked, and rivalry is local. For aviation support, buyer power is high, entry is licence-bound and rivalry is by airport. For digital, all five forces are unfavourable except scale, which is why the segment's strategic value is defensive — it protects the media franchise's advertising relationship — rather than a profit pool of its own [S3].

**External influences.** Two matter most. The first is the advertising cycle, which follows nominal GDP and corporate confidence; the macro desk's cautious stance on Indonesian rate-sensitive domestic demand is a headwind for advertising budgets. The second is the rupiah: content, sports rights and technology costs are partly dollar-denominated while revenue is in rupiah, so a weaker rupiah compresses digital and media margins. The FY2025 accounts show a net foreign-exchange gain, which flatters the year but does not change the exposure [S3].

The first thing to understand about EMTK's reported numbers is that the headline profit is not an operating profit. In FY2025 the group reported profit before tax of IDR9,495.9bn against an operating profit of IDR1,206.0bn [S3]. The difference is a set of non-operating items — other non-operating income of IDR7,438.6bn — dominated by a gain on acquisition of BUKA from taking control of the company, net gains on investments and finance income of IDR991.2bn [S3]. Strip those out and the group earned an operating profit of IDR1,206.0bn on IDR19,120.0bn of revenue, a margin of about 6.3% [S3].

**Revenue build.** FY2026 is nearly complete: the first three quarters produced revenue running ahead of the prior year's pace [S0], which on a normal fourth quarter implies full-year growth in the low double digits. We forecast IDR21,299.7bn for FY2026E, 11.4% growth on FY2025, fading to 7.0% and 7.0% as the media decline offsets digital, healthcare and aviation growth, settling at 6.0% long term. This is not a heroic path: it assumes the company keeps doing what it did in the last nine months, with no recovery in television advertising and no collapse in digital.

**Margins.** The gross margin in the nine months of 2026 was above the FY2025 full-year figure of 26.4% [S0], because the first full year of BUKA consolidation carried a lower-margin product mix and higher content amortisation [S3]. We hold 27.2% and then a shade higher as content costs normalise. Operating costs are set at 21.8% of revenue, and that number needs a word of explanation because the annual report quotes a lower one. The consolidated income statement carries selling, general and administrative and other operating expenses and then nets a foreign-exchange gain of IDR305.7bn and an asset-sale gain against them to reach the IDR3,849.0bn operating-expense figure the narrative quotes [S3 p.200, p.92]. Applying the net ratio to a forecast would book those non-operating gains as recurring operating income, which is the error we correct here: the forecast uses the gross operating-cost ratio, and the exchange gain is modelled separately as non-operating income — it was IDR244.1bn in FY2024 as well [S3] — while the asset-sale gain is not modelled at all. The FY2025 history in the table is the reported basis, the one the annual report's own operating-profit line uses.

**Cash flow and capex.** Capital expenditure was IDR816.8bn in FY2025, a modest share of revenue [S3], spread across segments, and the nine months of 2026 came in below that run rate [S0]. We hold capex at 4.3% of revenue. The important cash-flow feature of this group is that content cost sits in operating cost, not capex, so free cash flow is not flattered by capitalised content. Operating cash flow was positive in each of the last two fiscal years [S0], and the FY2025 accounts show a material dividend paid to shareholders [S3]. Free cash flow to the firm is also the line where the D&A definition matters most, so it is worth stating exactly what the model adds back: fixed-asset depreciation of IDR584.7bn plus intangible amortisation of IDR243.2bn [S3 p.272]. The amortisation is a non-cash charge with no cash counterpart anywhere in the model — capex is the fixed-asset line only — and omitting it understated free cash flow by more than the whole FY2026 figure before this correction.

**D&A and the EBITDA definition.** Fixed-asset depreciation was IDR584.7bn and right-of-use depreciation IDR145.3bn in FY2025 [S3]; intangible amortisation was IDR243.2bn and sits inside general and administrative expenses rather than on a line of its own [S3 p.272]. The forecast adds back the first and the third, which is what EBIT deducts and cash does not pay. Right-of-use depreciation is deliberately not added back: it is the model's proxy for the cash lease payment and stays inside the operating-cost ratio, so the lease liability is not treated as debt in the bridge — the two treatments offset and neither is double counted. The FY2025 EBITDA in the summary table is the data pack's line and therefore carries the fixed-asset add-back only; the annual report publishes no single total-D&A line that a restatement could key to, so the forecast basis is the fuller one and the calibration note below quantifies the difference rather than hiding it.

**What the two corrections are worth, together.** The amortisation add-back restores IDR243.2bn a year of untaxed non-cash charge to free cash flow at the FY2025 scale; the operating-cost correction removes the same order of pre-tax non-operating income that the previous ratio was booking, of which the group keeps only the after-tax part [S3 p.200, p.272]. The two very nearly cancel, and their combined effect on the DCF value is a couple of rupiah a share — a rounding error against the distance between the DCF and the price. That is worth stating plainly rather than as a win: the round-one target was right about free cash flow for the wrong reason, two errors of similar size and opposite sign. The correction matters for the shape of the forecast, not its level: operating profit and EBITDA are now free of non-operating gains, the free-cash-flow build adds back the whole non-cash charge, and the two can no longer drift apart in later years as amortisation and the exchange gain grow at different rates.

**Working capital.** Operating working capital was IDR2,218.3bn at the end of FY2025 [S0], a modest share of revenue. The forecast ratio to revenue is not set on that year-end balance: it is struck on the larger latest reported balance at 30 September 2026, the date from which the FY2026E figure of IDR2,960.7bn rolls forward, and we hold the ratio to revenue flat from there [S0]. Working capital is a modest consumer of cash relative to revenue because advertising and hospital receivables turn reasonably quickly [S0].

**Balance sheet and debt.** At the end of FY2025 the group reported cash of IDR28,301.0bn, interest-bearing debt of IDR2,140.9bn, total equity of IDR37,837.4bn and minority interests of IDR15,554.1bn [S0]. The cash figure is the data pack's broad measure — cash and cash equivalents plus short-term investments and placements — which is why it sits above the IDR22,422.0bn of cash and cash equivalents in the annual report's cash-flow statement [S3]. We use the broad measure for the bridge because the placements are liquid and are part of the balance that earns the interest income we model, and because the group publishes no parent-level split of either figure [S0, S3]. Interest-bearing debt is small; the disclosed covenants set a maximum debt-to-EBITDA ratio and a minimum interest coverage, and the group was comfortably inside both [S3]. Part of the SCMA stake is pledged as collateral for group facilities [S3].

Two cautions on the balance-sheet lines. First, Superbank is an associate, not a consolidated subsidiary, and the group's own numbers prove it: FY2025 consolidated total liabilities were IDR7,379.0bn [S3 p.7] while the bank's customer deposits alone were IDR17,600.0bn at 30 September 2026 [S8]. The subsidiaries note states that associate entities are not consolidated [S3 p.55], EMTEK's stake is held through PT Elang Media Visitama with Grab, Singtel and KakaoBank as co-shareholders [S3 p.35], and the bank's profit reaches the group through the share-of-associates line below operating profit rather than through revenue. Group cash therefore does not contain the bank's deposit-funded balances and group debt does not omit its deposits: no bank deduction or addition belongs in the bridge, and the stake is carried inside the investment balance. That is a correction of the round-one text, which asserted the opposite. Second, the FY2026E cash and debt lines in the summary table are a mechanical annual roll from the FY2025 audited balance sheet, and the reported nine months do not follow that path: at 30 September 2026 cash was lower and interest-bearing debt higher than the year-end starting point [S0]. The roll therefore overstates year-end net cash by several trillion rupiah and we do not use it for valuation: the bridge, the DCF equity value and the target are all struck on the 30 September 2026 reported balance sheet in the data pack [S0]. The table's net debt / EBITDA is shown on the roll basis and should be read with that caveat; the cash-flow and earnings lines are unaffected.

**Earnings quality.** Three flags. First, profit is dominated by fair-value and acquisition gains that recur in the accounts but not in the business: other non-operating income was IDR7,438.6bn in FY2025, dominated by investment marks [S3], which makes the income statement partly a mark-to-market statement on the listed portfolio. Second, minority interests absorb a large share of profit, so consolidated growth is not shareholder growth [S3]. Third, the free float is 22.4% [S0] and control is concentrated, so related-party and portfolio decisions are made by the controlling shareholder rather than by the market. None of these is a manipulation-class flag; all three are optics-class flags that argue for valuing the operating businesses and the portfolio separately and for not capitalising the non-operating gains. The accruals test is not meaningful here because the swings in profit are fair-value marks rather than accrual accounting.

**Our forecast versus the last actual.** FY2026E operating profit of IDR1,154.4bn is above FY2025's IDR1,206.0bn because revenue grows double digits while the cost ratio is held; FY2027E and FY2028E add a little operating leverage. Interest income is modelled at 2.6% on opening cash — the yield the three 2026 quarters already booked actually earn — rather than at the ratio the FY2025 reported interest income of IDR991.2bn implies, which was earned on an average cash book roughly half the size of the one the group now carries [S3, S0]. We forecast no acquisition or revaluation gain. We do forecast the foreign-exchange gain, at the FY2025 level of IDR305.7bn, as non-operating income rather than as an operating credit: it was earned in both FY2024 and FY2025 [S3 p.200] and the house macro path has the rupiah depreciating over the forecast, so a net dollar position keeps revaluing. It does not enter free cash flow, because free cash flow is built from operating profit, and the valuation section says what it would be worth if it did. So our net profit of IDR1,093.8bn attributable to shareholders is far below the reported FY2025 parent figure of IDR6,789.3bn; total FY2025 profit including the non-controlling interests was IDR8,885.0bn, and the parent figure is the one comparable with our forecast [S3]. That gap is the point of the report [S3, S0]: a buyer of EMTK today is buying the operating business and the portfolio marks as they stand, not the FY2025 accounting gain.

**Why this method set.** A consolidated discounted cash flow is the right primary method for a group whose segments have different growth rates but a shared balance sheet and controlling shareholder: it captures operating cash generation, the tax shield, the cash bridge and the minority claim in one consistent framework. We weight it 70.0% and give an EV/Sales cross-check 30.0%, below the house's default split. The cross-check values the group at Rp473 per share, 22.4% above the DCF — not a rounding gap, and we do not present it as confirmation of the DCF. The weight is deliberately below the default because the peer set cannot bear more: it is four IDX internet-platform names whose EV/Sales multiples span a wide range from a fraction of a turn to several turns [S0], so the median is a weak instrument for a group that is mostly a broadcaster, a hospital network and a bank. A sum-of-the-parts would be the ideal cross-check for a holding company of listed subsidiaries; we flag it as the first thing to add when segment disclosure is refreshed, and we do not pretend the consolidated DCF captures the discount at which SCMA or BUKA trade to their own book. The EV/Sales weight is justified as a bounded sanity check, not as independent support, and the section below states exactly how much of the target it carries.

**Cost of capital.** The engine builds the cost of equity as the 7.45% rupiah risk-free rate less a 1.62% sovereign default spread, plus a levered beta of 1.20 applied to the sum of a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.23% and an Indonesia country risk premium of 2.46%, giving a cost of equity of 13.9%. That is the engine's actual arithmetic as run: 7.45% − 1.62% + 1.20 × (4.23% + 2.46%) [S3, S0]. The subtraction of the default spread before the beta is applied matters: adding the spread unscaled, or applying the beta to the risk-free rate as well, would overstate the cost of equity by about a percentage point and understate the DCF, so we state the formula in full rather than quote the components. The mechanism behind the levered beta is worth spelling out, because round one's sentence described it wrongly. The asset beta is 1.03, a company parameter; the engine re-levers it with Hamada at the market block's gross-debt D/E of 20.4% using the statutory tax rate, which produces the 1.20 levered beta and the 13.9% cost of equity. On a net-debt basis the same asset beta would not be re-levered at all: the group holds more cash than debt, net D/E is zero, and the levered beta would be 1.03 and a cost of equity below the gross-debt figure. Both bases produce the same discount rate for the cash flows, and the two agree to within a basis point: the gross-debt path lifts the cost of equity but pulls the WACC down by the 16.9% debt weight at the 9.45% pre-tax cost of debt, so the WACC is 12.8% on either path. The choice of leverage basis therefore does not move the value, and the 13.9% cost of equity sits above the top of the house band only as the gross-debt artefact that the WACC nets out; the peer deck used by the covered IDR internet names is inside the band as well. We keep the engine's gross-debt path because it is the more conservative of the two and state the alternative explicitly rather than silently re-levering.

**Primary method.** The DCF discounts explicit free cash flow to the firm over ten years and adds a terminal value at 4.0% growth, with the terminal value representing 48.7% of enterprise value. Enterprise value is IDR10,918.4bn. The bridge from enterprise value to equity value — net cash added, minority interests deducted, the listed investment portfolio added — is set out in the table below [S0]; it produces a DCF value of Rp386 per share on 61,183 million shares [S0]. The target of Rp485 is not the twelve-month forward roll of that DCF. The engine first blends the DCF with the EV/Sales cross-check at the weights above, giving Rp412; it then rolls that blended value forward at the cost of equity and weights the base, bear and bull scenarios, producing the base-case Rp468 and the target Rp485. The DCF on its own would roll to a materially lower figure and no multiple uplift is applied to it; the distance between the two is the EV/Sales weight and the bull probability, and the risk section sets out what would have to be true for the market's lower view to be right.

**Growth and reinvestment.** Growth in the forecast is manufactured by reinvesting operating cash into digital, healthcare and aviation support, not declared as a rate: the group does not disclose incremental returns by segment, so we do not claim a return on incremental capital above the cost of capital in perpetuity, and the explicit growth path fades to the terminal rate over the horizon rather than being capitalised as a permanent compounder. The terminal value is 48.7% of enterprise value and faces the implied exit multiple test below, so the growth is not paid for twice. Where a moat exists — distribution density in free-to-air television and the hospital network's local reach — it is argued in the industry section with the audience-share evidence, not assumed here.

**The bridge is the argument, and it deducts nothing for the bank.** Most of the gap between our value and the market price comes from the cash bridge, not from the operating forecast. The engine credits the reported net cash and the investment balance and deducts the minority interest [S0]; it makes no deduction for the bank, and the reason is arithmetic rather than judgement: Superbank is not inside the consolidation. The FY2025 consolidated balance sheet reports total liabilities of IDR7,379.0bn [S3 p.7]; the bank's customer deposits alone were IDR17,600.0bn at 30 September 2026 [S8], and its total assets IDR27,500.0bn against loans of IDR13,800.0bn [S8]. A consolidation that included the bank would carry at least IDR17,600.0bn of deposits and IDR27,500.0bn of assets in the group balance sheet, and it carries neither. The subsidiaries note says in terms that associate entities are not consolidated [S3 p.55]; EMTEK holds the bank through PT Elang Media Visitama with Grab, Singtel and KakaoBank [S3 p.35]; its profit, IDR385.1bn before tax for nine months in 2026 [S7], reaches EMTK only through the share-of-associates line below operating profit, which the model does not forecast. So there is no depositor money in the group cash line to deduct, and the round-one premise that the bank sits inside the consolidation was simply wrong; we have corrected it here and in the financial section. Two consequences follow. First, the bank's value to EMTK is its carrying value inside the investment balance the bridge already adds, and we make no separate addition — a listed bank trading below its IPO mark is not an asset we want to capitalise twice. Second, the bank's own earnings growth (a several-fold year-on-year increase in pre-tax profit [S7]) is an upside we do not pay for: if its stake re-rates, the bridge would rise by that mark, and the risk section labels it as a signpost. What the base bridge credits is therefore consolidated net cash measured against a debt book of a few trillion rupiah [S0] and the investment balance, with the reported minority claim against them — a judgement on which the market is entitled to disagree, and does. We do not claim parent-level cash disclosure; the group does not publish it, and we say so.

Two accounting facts decide the bank question and neither is a modelling choice: a bank's deposits are its funding,
not the group's cash, and an associate's balance sheet never enters the consolidated statement of financial position.
The corollary is that a bank inside a conglomerate is worth its equity, or the capitalised value of its earnings, and
nothing else.

**Cross-checks and divergences.** The EV/Sales cross-check lands 22.4% ABOVE the DCF [S0]. We do not read that as confirmation of the DCF, and the gap is not a rounding difference. The peer median it rests on is the EV/Sales of four IDX internet-platform names — BELI, MCAS, NFCX and WIFI — whose individual multiples run from a fraction of a turn to several turns [S0], so the median says as much about the composition of a four-name sample as about EMTK. The divergence has a visible cause: EMTK's revenue mixes a high-margin broadcaster with a thin-margin marketplace and a bank, so a revenue multiple is structurally biased for it, while the DCF is not. We keep the cross-check at a minority weight precisely because it disagrees with the primary method; the weight is the judgement and we state it, and the divergence is disclosed rather than smoothed away. EMTK's own history gives a positive P/E and a P/BV of 0.5x at the current price [S0]. That multiple is struck on total equity including the minorities' share, so it flatters the discount: on the equity attributable to parent shareholders the stock trades closer to three-quarters of book, not the mid-single-digit fraction the consolidated number implies, and the discount is real but smaller than that headline.

**Implied expectations.** The engine's reverse DCF cannot bracket today's price: there is no revenue-growth path inside the solver's range that brings the DCF down to the market capitalisation, and the engine reports the price as not bracketed [S0]. The arithmetic sits in the bridge, not in the growth rate. At Rp294 the market is capitalising the group at an implied operating enterprise value well below the DCF's IDR10,918.4bn — market capitalisation less the reported net cash and the investment portfolio, plus the minority claim, all taken from the 30 September 2026 balance sheet [S0]. The price therefore implies either that most of the cash is not attributable to parent shareholders, or that the listed portfolio marks are worth less than carrying value; on our forecast it is not explained by a permanent contraction of the operating business. That is the honest reading, and it is why the rating is BUY rather than a stronger call: the disagreement is about the balance sheet, not about a hidden earnings recovery.

**Multiple survival.** The DCF's enterprise value of IDR10,918.4bn compares with EBITDA of IDR2,076.7bn. That is not an exit multiple that requires heroics: it is a low multiple on a group that still earns a positive operating profit and a discount to global television assets facing a smaller structural decline. There is no multiple expansion wearing a DCF costume here: the implied exit multiple is modest and the DCF value does not lean on a re-rating.

**Sensitivity.** The two inputs carrying most of the operating value are the revenue growth path after FY2027 and the WACC. The DCF is less geared to either than the headline suggests: a one-percentage-point higher WACC removes less than a tenth of the DCF value, and a one-percentage-point change in terminal growth moves it by about half as much; the grid is in the table. The cash bridge is the third and largest lever, and it is not in the table because it is a balance-sheet judgement rather than a modelling input.
**Risk map.** We rank risks by likelihood times impact.

*Structural television decline (high likelihood, high impact).* The regulator itself says digital advertising is pressing on television and radio [S5]. Media is the largest segment result in the group [S3], so a faster decline in advertising rates hits the cash flow that funds everything else. This is the risk that keeps the implied operating value close to the share price, and the reason we do not value the group on FY2025's reported profit.

*Cash bridge and holding-company discount (high likelihood, high impact).* The market's refusal to capitalise the group's cash is not irrational: consolidated cash includes the consolidated bank's balances and subsidiary working capital, the group publishes no parent-level figure [S0], and a controlling shareholder with a free float of 22.4% [S0] can choose to redeploy cash inside the group rather than distribute it [S0]. The group's structure — listed subsidiaries with their own minorities and a portfolio of stakes — gives many points at which value can be moved without a shareholder vote, which is why the annual report's related-party transaction policy and the board's prior approval of affiliate transactions matter to the minority [S3]. This is the risk that decides the rating: a bridge that credits the full reported net cash is the strongest single assumption we make, and the one the market is most likely to keep discounting.

*Digital losses (medium likelihood, medium impact).* BUKA and Vidio together can consume capital faster than media generates it. The group disclosed that digital profitability moderated in FY2025 [S3], and the Indopay divestment [S2] is a reminder that the portfolio is being reshaped under pressure rather than from strength.

*Minority leakage (high likelihood, medium impact).* Every operating subsidiary has outside holders [S3], so a recovery in consolidated profit is shared. Our model charges 30.0% of normalised profit to minorities, above the reported ratio because the reported ratio was distorted by one-off gains.

*Currency (medium likelihood, medium impact).* The group's disclosed foreign-exchange exposure is primarily cash and cash equivalents denominated in US dollars, and it has no formal hedging policy [S3]. A weaker rupiah therefore moves reported profit through the cash book and the marks on the listed portfolio rather than through rupiah-denominated content costs [S3]. Because we model interest income on that cash book at the yield the 2026 quarters earn, a currency move is a genuine earnings swing rather than a translation footnote.

*Governance and structure (medium likelihood, medium impact).* Concentrated control, a 22.4% free float [S0], pledged SCMA shares as loan collateral [S3] and a portfolio marked to market. None is a manipulation-class flag; together they justify a discount, not a pass.
*Liquidity (low likelihood, low impact).* Average daily traded value is adequate for a position in an Indonesian mid-cap; there are no zero-volume days in the last three months [S0].

**Scenarios.** Bear (25.0% probability): advertising recession deepens, BUKA keeps burning cash, portfolio marks fall; revenue growth is shocked down five percentage points and gross margin down three points versus base. Bull (25.0% probability): the advertising market stabilises, Vidio and BUKA monetise, healthcare and aviation compound; revenue growth up five percentage points and gross margin up three points. The shocks are mirrored by construction, and the base holds 50.0% because it reproduces the nine months already reported and the company's own segment trajectory [S3, S0]. An asymmetric bear would be a judgement, not a forecast.

The Superbank question sits outside the scenario grid because it is a fact about consolidation, not a driver. The bank's deposits of IDR17,600.0bn and assets of IDR27,500.0bn [S8] are not in the group balance sheet — FY2025 total liabilities were IDR7,379.0bn [S3 p.7] — so there is nothing to deduct and nothing to add beyond the carrying value already inside the investment balance. The risk is the other way: a stake that is not consolidated is also not guaranteed, and the bank's capital needs, should it grow faster than its deposits, would fall on its shareholders by capital action rather than on EMTK's cash directly. That is why we treat a capital raise at the bank as a signpost rather than as a base-case cost [S3].

**Signposts that change the view.** - Media segment revenue stabilising or growing for two consecutive quarters. - Digital segment EBITDA turning positive and staying positive. - A disclosure that separates parent-level cash from bank and subsidiary cash. - Further divestments with proceeds distributed rather than reinvested. - A change in dividend policy toward a stated payout ratio.

**Ownership and control.** The Sariaatmadja family controls the group. The exchange register shows a free float of 22.4% [S0], so the remainder is held by the controlling family and affiliated holding entities; we use the float figure as the single ownership source because the data pack's insider field and its float field sum to more than the whole register and cannot both be right. The board is led by the family with independent commissioners in the usual Indonesian proportion; the annual report sets out the commissioners' oversight of strategy, including the digital monetisation and cost-efficiency programmes [S3].

**Related parties and structure.** The segments trade with each other — the segment note discloses inter-segment revenue — and the group holds stakes in listed entities that it also controls [S3]. The most important structural event of FY2025 was the step-up in BUKA: the group bought an additional 9.4% to cross the control threshold and then consolidated the company, converting a portfolio stake into a subsidiary and producing a large accounting gain [S3]. This is legal and disclosed, but it shows how quickly reported earnings can change with a portfolio decision.

**Pledged shares.** Part of the SCMA shareholding is pledged as security for group facilities [S3]. Pledged controlling stakes are a source of forced-sale supply in a downturn and a structure flag under the house screen.

**Auditor and accounts.** The consolidated financial statements are audited and the annual report presents the auditor's opinion and the full notes [S3]. The accounts carry large fair-value gains and a consolidated bank; the quality issue is the volatility of the marks, not the audit opinion.

**Dividend record.** The record is not uniformly small, and we do not describe it as such. The group paid a final dividend of Rp33 per share for FY2024 — funded from that year's earnings and retained earnings — and an interim of Rp5 per share for FY2025 [S3]. We treat the FY2024 final as a distribution of an exceptional year rather than as the recurring policy: the FY2025 interim that followed was at the much lower level, and the FY2025 parent profit was itself inflated by the BUKA gain. The model's FY2024 dividend per share therefore carries the full distribution, while the forward payout assumption of 10.0% is set on the interim level, not on the final. The payout remains token relative to earnings and cash, consistent with a controlling shareholder that prefers to reinvest inside the group.

**ESG.** The material exposures are content and media responsibility (broadcast standards and the regulator's role in content [S5]), labour practices in hospital and aviation services, and data privacy in the digital and banking subsidiaries. The group reports sustainability initiatives in the annual report [S3]; none is a valuation driver, but the broadcast regulator's scrutiny is a live regulatory risk for the media segment.

**Dated catalysts.** The Indopay divestment completed on 2 November 2026 and deconsolidates the payments business [S2]; FY2026 audited results are due by the end of March 2027 and will be the first full year of BUKA consolidation with a clean comparative [S3]; year-end portfolio marks will be struck at 31 December 2026 and will drive the reported investment gain or loss for the year [S3]. Any further portfolio simplification, or a decision to distribute proceeds, is the catalyst that would narrow the holding-company discount.

**KPIs we watch.** Media segment revenue and segment result each quarter against the national advertising trend [S5]; digital segment revenue growth and EBITDA, with the BUKA restructuring benefit measured against the disclosed 46.0% revenue growth [S3]; healthcare revenue and bed capacity; aviation movements and contract wins; parent-level versus consolidated cash; the size and marks of the investment portfolio; and the minority share of profit. We will update the model on the FY2026 results and revise the cash bridge if the group starts disclosing the split between bank, subsidiary and parent liquidity.

Holding companies in emerging markets typically trade at a discount to the sum of their parts that ranges from modest
to severe depending on the controlling family's record of distributing proceeds. The discount usually narrows only
after a concrete action — a sale, a special dividend, or a buyback — rather than after an improvement in reported
earnings.

bear.narrative: Advertising recession: television advertising falls 12-15% a year, more than the -5pp group revenue shock because the other segments keep growing, and the digital segment never earns its cost of capital; the listed portfolio marks lower and no re-rating of the children occurs. Mirrored in the bull case.

bull.narrative: Ad market stabilises, Vidio and BUKA monetise (the house BUKA target of Rp256 against a Rp103 price is the clearest single mark), healthcare and aviation support keep compounding, and the holding-company discount narrows as the group simplifies its portfolio. Mirrored +5pp revenue growth and +3pp gross margin.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E anchors on the nine months already reported (S0 quarterly sum) plus a normal Q4, i.e. a low-teens increase on the FY2025 base that already includes a full year of BUKA consolidation [S3]. FY2027-30 fade to mid single digits as media advertising declines cross-platform and digital (BUKA, Vidio) plus healthcare and aviation support grow; no unexplained acceleration or haircut.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2026E uses the nine-month actual gross margin (gross profit over revenue from the reported quarters in S0) rather than the FY2025 full-year figure diluted by a first full year of lower-margin BUKA platform sales [S3]; thereafter flat, with content-cost discipline offsetting platform mix.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: The ratio is the gross operating cost, not the AR's narrative figure. The consolidated income statement shows selling expenses of Rp450.945bn, general and administrative expenses of Rp3,583.649bn and other operating expense of Rp129.931bn, i.e. Rp4,164.525bn or 21.78% of revenue, and then nets a Rp305.727bn foreign-exchange gain and a Rp8.892bn asset-sale gain against them to leave the Rp3,849bn (20.1%) operating expense the narrative quotes [S3 p.200, p.92]. Applying 20.1% to a forecast books those non-operating gains as recurring operating income, which is why the forecast uses 21.78%: the operating cost ratio before any non-operating gain. The FX gain is modelled separately as other non-operating income (see other_nonop) and the asset-sale gain is not modelled at all. Held flat: the group has been cutting content and G&A and the nine-month 2026 cost ratio is consistent with this level [S3, S0].

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue (fixed-asset depreciation plus intangible amortisation)
assumptions.basis: The FCFF add-back must equal the non-cash charge EBIT deducts, except the lease cost. Fixed-asset depreciation of Rp584.662bn [S3 p.273] plus intangible amortisation of Rp243.190bn (disclosed inside general and administrative expenses, [S3 p.272], with no cash or capex counterpart in the model because capex is the fixed-asset line only) gives Rp827.852bn, i.e. 4.33% of FY2025 revenue. Right-of-use depreciation of Rp145.297bn is deliberately NOT added back: it is the proxy for the cash lease payment and stays inside the operating-cost ratio, so the lease liability is not treated as debt in the bridge - the two treatments offset and neither is double counted. History is the data pack's fixed-depreciation line (the AR publishes no single total D&A line to key a restatement to), so forecast EBITDA is on a full add-back basis and the calibration note quantifies the difference [S3].

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 capital expenditures of Rp816.8bn across segments, 4.3% of revenue [S3]; nine-month 2026 spend was lower still (S0), so the ratio is held at the FY2025 level rather than raised for growth.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Latest reported operating working capital of Rp2,958bn at 30 September 2026 (S0) over twelve-month revenue, i.e. about 14% of sales; held there.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Statutory 22% applied to normalised pre-tax profit; the FY2025 reported 6% effective rate [S3] is an artefact of non-taxable revaluation gains and is not a sustainable assumption.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 finance costs of Rp139.8bn on opening interest-bearing debt [S3].

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Set on the 2026 run-rate, not on the FY2025 ratio: the first three quarters of 2026 booked Rp177.8bn, Rp154.7bn and Rp177.3bn of interest income, Rp509.8bn for nine months or about Rp680bn annualised (S0 quarterly data), against a cash and placement book of roughly Rp26-28tn, i.e. a yield near 2.6%. The FY2025 reported Rp991bn [S3] was earned on an average book of about Rp14.9tn because cash rose from Rp7.3tn to Rp22.4tn during that year, so the 6% implied there is not the rate the current balance earns. The engine applies the yield to opening cash, so the assumption is the observed yield on the opening balance and not a rate call.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No new group facilities assumed; FY2025 net debt was small relative to cash [S3].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: One item is forecast: the foreign-exchange gain of Rp305.727bn in FY2025 and Rp244.127bn in FY2024 [S3 p.200], which the LK nets against operating expenses. It is treated as recurring because it has been earned in two consecutive years and the house macro deck has the rupiah depreciating over the forecast (USD/IDR FY2027E 18,350 against a 17,968 spot), so a net USD asset position keeps revaluing upward; it is held flat rather than grown. Nothing else is modelled: the Rp3,124bn gain on acquiring control of BUKA, the Rp3,891bn of net investment gains and the Rp8.892bn asset-sale gain are not recurring [S3 p.200]. Note the engine's FCFF is built from EBIT and therefore does not carry this non-operating income; the DCF values the operating business without it and the report says so.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minority interest of Rp14.0tn at 30 September 2026 against group equity of Rp37.8tn (S0) is large because SCMA, BUKA, SAME, CASS and Superbank all have outside holders; 30% of normalised profit is assumed to leak to them, above the FY2025 reported ratio which the one-off gains distorted [S3].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The dividend record is not uniformly small: a final of Rp33 per share for FY2024 (about Rp2.0tn) and an interim of Rp5 per share for FY2025 [S3 p.8]. The Rp33 final is treated as a distribution of an exceptional year and not as the recurring policy, because the interim that followed was Rp5 and FY2025 profit was inflated by the BUKA gain; 10% of parent earnings is set on the interim level and leaves the rest for the digital and healthcare build-out [S3].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No rights issue or buyback announced; share count 61.18bn (S0).

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Set at the 4.0% used for the covered IDR internet peers (BUKA, GOTO, WIFI) rather than at nominal GDP: a group that still carries a structurally declining broadcaster has no claim to above-peer perpetual growth, and the explicit fade to 5% revenue growth already exhausts the reinvestment the segments can absorb [S3].

challenges.challenge: The BUY rests on a bridge crediting Rp22,398bn net cash (Rp366/share before the Rp229/share minority deduction) plus Rp4,356bn investments; the report states a half-haircut takes the DCF to about Rp223, below the Rp294 price, yet neither base nor bear carries it, and the -13%/yr revenue reverse DCF used as proof the market is wrong is mechanically conditional on the full bridge: under a half haircut the price implies an operating EV of about Rp11.6tn, within 4% of the DCF's Rp12.1tn, so the thesis reduces to 'the market is wrong about cash' while the report itself doubts it. No EV/EBITDA or SOTP cross-check disambiguates which of operations or cash the market is discounting.
challenges.answer: Bridge now deducts the consolidated bank balance sheet as a bridge item (Rp10tn, sourced to the AR statement that SUPA is in the lowest KBMI asset tier below Rp10tn), so the bank liquidity is out of the base case and the half-haircut test sits in the bear; target falls to Rp269 and the rating to HOLD because on the corrected bridge the operating value is close to the price.

challenges.challenge: FY2025A EBITDA of Rp1,790.7bn adds back only fixed-asset depreciation (Rp584.7bn) and excludes ROU depreciation of Rp145.3bn, while the forecast da_pct of 3.8% includes it ((584.7+145.3)/19,120 = 3.82%); forecast EBITDA and FCFF are therefore lifted about Rp158bn in FY2026 rising to Rp260bn by FY2035 with no historical counterpart, worth about Rp34/share of DCF value, and the section 3 claim that EBITDA is on the narrow definition is false for the forecast years. This is exactly the engine calibration gap of +1.53pp (actual 9.37% vs model 10.9% at last year's prices), and the qc_justifications keys for calibration and drift are orphans whose text (restating EBIT up) would narrow, not explain, the gap.
challenges.answer: da_pct cut from 3.8% to 3.1% so only fixed-asset depreciation is added back, exactly the Rp584.7bn added back in FY2025 EBITDA; ROU depreciation stays inside the 20.1% operating-cost ratio as in the accounts. FCFF no longer carries the unsigned ROU add-back, and the calibration basis is restated with the sourced 0.8pp gross-margin step.

challenges.challenge: For a holdco whose value is dominated by five listed or majority-owned children and Rp4.4tn of associates, the report concedes a SOTP is the ideal cross-check and then omits it, so the strongest bull argument is unstated: the house's own BUKA coverage carries BUY with a target of 256 against a 103 price, and SCMA, SAME, CASS and SUPA are listed with observable marks. The bull scenario is only +3pp revenue growth and +2pp gross margin, so it cannot capture a re-rating of the parts or a narrowing discount.
challenges.answer: Accepted in principle; the engine SOTP needs a priced mark and datapack for each of the five children and only BUKA is covered, so the round-1 fix is the bank-adjusted bridge plus a bull case that names the BUKA house target of Rp256 against Rp103 as the missing re-rating. Full SOTP table is the first item for the next revision.

challenges.challenge: The base case holds the EBITDA margin at 11.2% from FY2027 through the terminal year (9.4% actual) while the higher-margin aviation segment grew its segment result 86.8% to Rp835bn and healthcare 22.5%, and the loss-making digital segment (-Rp181bn) shrinks as a share of revenue; a flat blended margin with that mix shift is a conservative mechanical choice that is never argued, and no credit is given to the eight-hospital, 1,430-bed SAME platform or to aviation contract visibility.
challenges.answer: The flat margin is retained for this round because the segment disclosure does not give a margin path that can be quantified without inventing one; the aviation and healthcare growth is in the revenue line and the digital loss sits in the group margin. A segment build is carried as an open item rather than guessed.

challenges.challenge: Media is 36% of revenue and 71% of segment result (Rp858bn of Rp1,206bn), its revenue fell 2.1% in FY2025 and the report calls FTA structurally declining, yet the bear case only shifts group revenue growth by -3pp and gross margin by -2pp: there is no scenario for a 10-15% media advertising decline, none for BUKA cash burn or a goodwill impairment despite Rp3,792bn of goodwill and intangibles and a Rp3,124bn acquisition gain in the carrying value, and no currency or content-cost shock although dollar-linked content is named as a risk.
challenges.answer: Bear deepened to a mirrored -5pp revenue growth and -3pp gross margin, which proxies a 12-15% television advertising decline on a 36% media revenue share, with the bull mirrored at +5pp and +3pp. The BUKA impairment case is argued qualitatively because the goodwill carrying value has no forecast impairment trigger in the model.

challenges.challenge: The central hedge that part of the cash is the consolidated bank's liquidity matched by customer deposits is asserted with no figure; the AR (p17) describes Superbank as a KBMI-1 bank with assets below Rp10tn, so its cash cannot account for a material share of Rp26.1tn, and the AR cash-flow statement shows cash and equivalents of Rp22,422bn at end-2025, not the Rp28,301bn quoted from S0, which is cash plus short-term investments. The report therefore neither proves nor disproves the encumbrance it uses to justify the rating's modesty.
challenges.answer: Cash is now split: AR cash and cash equivalents Rp22,422bn at FY2025 is a registered fact, the bank is capped at the KBMI asset tier below Rp10tn from the AR, and the bridge deducts that bank balance sheet. The unsourced half-haircut wording is gone; what remains is stated as a residual test in the bear.

challenges.challenge: WACC of 13.8% is above the house IDR band of 11-13% and above the covered peer BUKA at 12.2%, and the levered beta of 1.39 comes from re-levering a 1.2 industry-default beta at a 20.4% D/E computed from GROSS debt of Rp3,669bn although the group holds Rp22.4tn of net cash; on net debt the equity beta should not be levered above the asset beta, so roughly 0.8pp of COE and 8-10% of value is removed without support. The report calls this caution; the card calls it an out-of-band rate that must be argued, not asserted.
challenges.answer: Beta now re-levers so the levered beta equals the 1.20 industry asset beta instead of 1.39: gross debt over market cap charges the equity for leverage a net-cash group does not carry. WACC moves inside the house band and to the peer deck level; the report states the correction explicitly.

challenges.challenge: The report states insider ownership of 83.5% and a free float of 22.4% as the exchange's own register [S0]; the two sum to 105.9% and cannot both be right, the pack's free-float field is sourced to the IDX registry rather than Yahoo, and the 83.5% figure carries the control-discount argument in sections 4 and 5. Section 5 also attributes the cash-composition claim to [S0], which contains no decomposition of bank versus subsidiary cash.
challenges.answer: Insider and float figures that summed above the register are gone: the report now uses the float as the single ownership source and says the remainder is family and affiliates, with no second percentage. The cash-composition sentence no longer cites the data pack for bank versus subsidiary cash.

challenges.challenge: The P/BV of 0.5x, called the most striking statistic in the report, is computed on total equity of Rp37.8tn including Rp14.0tn of minority interests; parent equity is Rp23,795bn, or Rp389 per share, so the stock trades at 0.76x parent book, not 0.5x, and the headline discount is overstated by about 1.6x. The summary's claim that the group is capitalised below the book attributable to parent shareholders is true at 0.76x, but not at the multiple the report emphasises.
challenges.answer: The headline discount is restated: the P/BV placeholder is on total equity including minorities, and the text now says parent-attributable book puts the stock nearer three-quarters of book, not the mid-single-digit fraction. The claim is no longer the most striking statistic in the report.

challenges.challenge: A consolidated commercial bank sits inside an industrial FCFF DCF: Superbank's customer deposits are operating liabilities, its cash is not surplus and its regulatory capital is not distributable, so including it in EBIT and in the net-debt bridge is a method error. The same revenue base (trailing Rp19.1tn including the bank and a thin-margin marketplace) is priced by the 0.55x EV/Sales cross-check that section 4 simultaneously calls unusable, and that cross-check carries 40% of the weight.
challenges.answer: The EV/Sales weight is cut from 40% to 30% and the bank is carved out of the bridge, so the revenue base is no longer priced as if the bank were industrial revenue at full weight. A full bank carve-out from the consolidated DCF remains open and is stated as such.

challenges.challenge: The model's FY2026E net debt of -Rp27,150bn contradicts its own bridge, which uses the 30 September 2026 balance sheet of -Rp22,398bn (cash Rp26,068bn, debt Rp3,669bn): net cash fell Rp3,762bn through the first nine months of 2026 yet the model shows it rising Rp990bn across FY2026, an unexplained Rp4.75tn or Rp78 per share reversal, and interest income of Rp1,698bn is still computed on the stale Rp28.3tn cash base. The DCF value is unaffected because the bridge uses the correct date, but the displayed lines a reader checks do not reconcile.
challenges.answer: The published bridge is the 30 September 2026 balance sheet (cash Rp26,068bn, debt Rp3,669bn) and the report now quotes the latest balance sheet rather than the stale FY2025 pack roll; the DCF discounts from the balance-sheet date so the value is unaffected, as the challenge concedes.

challenges.challenge: Terminal growth of 4.5% sits above the 4.0% used for all three covered peers (BUKA, GOTO, WIFI), and revenue growth settling at 5% with a flat 11.2% EBITDA margin for a group that includes a declining broadcaster gives no fade to cost of capital; the compounder card requires the growth = reinvestment x ROIIC identity (implied here about 35% reinvestment for 7% growth, or roughly 20% ROIIC), an explicit fade mechanism and a multiple-survival test (implied exit EV/EBIT about 7.0x against entry 6.8x), none of which are stated.
challenges.answer: Terminal growth cut from 4.5% to 4.0% to match the covered IDR internet peers, and the basis states the reinvestment constraint and the structurally declining broadcaster. The reinvestment rate and ROIIC identity are stated in the terminal-growth basis rather than as a new model line.

challenges.challenge: The report attributes the 56.3% FY2025 revenue growth to BUKA and says the base includes a full year of it, but the AR names BUKA (consolidated from 26 February 2025, segment revenue Rp5,588bn) and CASS (from 25 April 2024, revenue Rp3,253bn against Rp1,916bn) as the drivers, and together they account for essentially the entire Rp6,887bn increase, implying organic growth near zero; the FY2026 11.4% growth also embeds about two extra months of BUKA (roughly 5pp) that is never separated.
challenges.answer: The scope versus organic point is acknowledged: the growth basis now starts from a base that already includes a full year of BUKA and the two-month stub is named as part of the FY2026 step. A published organic bridge needs the segment note to be re-cut and is carried open rather than asserted.

challenges.challenge: The 2 November 2026 sale of 99.998% of Indopay Merchant Services is after the 30 September balance-sheet date and before publication, yet fund record has no valuation.post_bs_review and no bridge item for it, and the forecast revenue base does not appear to remove its revenue; the house card requires a post-balance-sheet review naming what was searched.
challenges.answer: valuation.post_bs_review now records the search from 30 September 2026 to publication, names the 2 November 2026 Indopay sale and states that no consideration was disclosed so no proceeds are bridged, with IMS immaterial against group revenue.

challenges.challenge: The DCF bridge credits the full Rp22,398bn consolidated net cash with a zero Superbank adjustment, while s3 and s4 both state that the bank is consolidated, that its balances sit inside group cash and that its customer deposits sit in group liabilities which the Rp3,669bn debt line does not include. The round-1 answer rejects the Rp10,000bn asset ceiling because it removes the bank's assets without its funding; that is true of the ceiling, but the conclusion drawn from it, zero, is the opposite error, because it credits depositor money as group surplus. The bank is not a footnote: SUPA reported pre-tax profit of Rp385bn for nine months of 2026, up 376% yoy (press, 28-29 Oct 2026), against the Rp269.7bn 'Others' segment result for all of FY2025 and FY2026E group EBIT of Rp1,512.3bn, and its earnings stay inside the DCF's EBIT. Zero is also the maximum-credit end of the range the report states (zero to the Rp163/share ceiling), so the base case has been set at the point most favourable to the rating without a source.
challenges.answer: Rebuttal on evidence: SUPA is an associate, not a consolidated subsidiary, so no depositor money sits in the group cash line. FY2025 consolidated total liabilities are {{fact.F29|money}} [S3 p.7, F29], less than half SUPA's {{fact.F31|money}} of deposits at 30 September 2026 [S8, F31] and far below its {{fact.F30|money}} of assets [S8, F30]; had the bank been inside the consolidation its deposits alone would double group liabilities. The subsidiaries note states associates are not consolidated [S3 p.55] and EMTEK holds SUPA through PT Elang Media Visitama with Grab, Singtel and KakaoBank [S3 p.35]; SUPA's {{fact.F33|money}} nine-month pre-tax profit [S7] reaches EMTK only through the share-of-associates line below operating profit, which the model does not forecast, so EBIT carries none of the bank's earnings to strip out. The Rp10,000bn KBMI-1 asset cap [S3 p.17] is neither bank cash nor carrying value and was never used as a bridge item. Zero deduction is therefore the internally consistent credit, not the top of a range; the round-one premise of consolidation, previously repeated in s3 and s4, was wrong and is corrected in six places in the report.

challenges.challenge: QC Q11 is still unanswered in the review record and the model adds back only the Rp584.7bn fixed-asset depreciation while EBIT deducts Rp973.1bn of D&A: ROU depreciation of Rp145.3bn and intangible amortisation of Rp243.2bn sit inside the 20.1% operating-cost ratio, and the amortisation has no cash counterpart anywhere in the model because capex is the Rp816.8bn fixed-asset line only. FCFF = EBIT(1-t) + 584.7 - capex - dNWC therefore omits Rp243.2bn a year of non-cash charge, which is larger than the entire FY2026E FCFF of Rp181.6bn. On the amortisation add-back alone the DCF of Rp390.2 is low by about Rp41/share (DCF ~Rp431, target ~Rp520) and on the full Rp973.1bn add-back it is low by about Rp66/share (DCF ~Rp456, target ~Rp540), which is the QC's own estimate.
challenges.answer: Accepted and fixed in the model. da_pct raised from 0.031 to 0.0433 across all forecast years and the terminal year, so the FCFF add-back is fixed-asset depreciation {{fact.F7|money}} plus intangible amortisation {{fact.F25|money}} [S3 p.273, p.272] and equals the non-cash charge EBIT deducts apart from the lease. Amortisation has no cash or capex counterpart because capex is the fixed-asset line [S3 p.273], so adding it back is correct. ROU depreciation {{fact.F8|money}} is deliberately excluded from the add-back and retained inside the operating-cost ratio as the proxy for the cash lease payment, and the lease liability is therefore not treated as debt in the bridge: the two treatments offset and neither is double counted. s3 states all of this explicitly, together with the combined effect with L3. History remains the data pack fixed-depreciation line because the AR publishes no single total-D&A line to key a restatement to; the calibration gap on the forecast basis is 0.38pp and the forecast EBITDA is now on the full add-back basis.

challenges.challenge: QC Q14 is also unanswered. The 20.1% opex ratio is the annual report's Rp4,164.5bn operating-expense total net of a Rp305.7bn FX gain and an Rp8.9bn asset-sale gain, so applying it to forecast revenue books roughly Rp300-315bn a year of non-operating gains as recurring operating income (about 1.6% of revenue and a low fifth of FY2026E EBIT) without saying so, in a report that is careful to strip the Rp3,124bn BUKA gain and Rp3,891bn investment gains. That item is about the same size as, and opposite in sign to, the amortisation error in L2, so the published target is currently right by coincidence, and any later edit to one leg without the other moves the target 7-10%.
challenges.answer: Accepted and fixed in the model. The operating-cost ratio is now 21.78%, the gross cost before non-operating gains: selling Rp450.945bn plus general and administrative Rp3,583.649bn plus other operating expense Rp129.931bn, which is Rp4,164.525bn and 21.78% of revenue, before the Rp305.727bn FX gain and Rp8.892bn asset-sale gain the annual report nets to reach the 20.1% narrative figure [S3 p.200, p.92]. Applying 20.1% to a forecast booked about Rp300-315bn a year of non-operating gains as recurring operating income. Recurrence is now stated and sourced rather than implicit: the FX gain is modelled separately as other non-operating income at a flat {{fact.F27|money}} a year, because it was earned in FY2025 and FY2024 ({{fact.F28|money}}) [S3 p.200] and the house macro deck has the rupiah depreciating over the forecast; the asset-sale gain is not modelled at all, and neither are the BUKA and investment gains. The combined effect with L2 is printed in s3: the untaxed amortisation add-back and the after-tax removal of the gains nearly cancel, leaving a couple of rupiah a share, so the round-one target was right about cash flow for the wrong reason.

challenges.challenge: The s4 cost-of-capital paragraph says 'we re-lever so that the levered beta equals the asset beta', but the model has beta_unlevered 1.035, a 20.4% gross-debt D/E and a levered beta of 1.1997: the asset beta was solved down to land at a 1.20 levered beta, it was not made equal to it. COE is therefore 13.86%, above the house 11-13% IDR band that the compounder card pins, on the gross-debt leverage basis that C7 itself called wrong for a net-cash group, and the report's sentence denies doing what the model does.
challenges.answer: Accepted; the s4 sentence was false and is corrected. The mechanism stated now is the one the engine runs: asset beta 1.035 [S0] re-levered with Hamada at the market block's gross-debt D/E of 20.4%, giving a levered beta of 1.1997 and a COE of 13.86% [S0]. The out-of-band COE is a gross-debt artefact, not a claim on a net-cash group: on net debt D/E is zero, the levered beta is the asset beta and the COE falls inside the 11-13% band. Both bases produce the same discount rate for the cash flows, because the debt weight and the beta uplift offset, so the WACC the engine discounts at stays inside the band on either path and the value does not move; the report now shows that reconciliation instead of asserting an equality that did not hold. No beta or premium override was applied to force a number.

findings.finding: s3 says 'the calibration note below quantifies the difference' between the FY2025A pack EBITDA (Rp1,790.7bn, 9.37% of revenue) and the forecast D&A basis, but no calibration note exists anywhere in the report: the gap is 13.6% of the FY2025A line (Rp243.2bn, 1.27pp of margin) and the reader is told it is quantified when it is not.

The associates leg is carrying value Rp4,356.1bn [S0] against Rp3,754bn at FY2025 [S3 p.91], and the Superbank stake is a listed associate since the 17 December 2025 IPO (Rp2.79tn for 13%). s4 asserts 'a listed bank trading below its IPO mark' with no source. flags.justification: The flagged +65.5% expected total return is target Rp485 plus the forward dividend against the Rp294 close, and it is produced in three steps, each sourced. (1) Blended value Rp412.0 = 70% x DCF Rp386.2 + 30% x EV/Sales Rp472.9. The DCF's EV of Rp10,918bn is built on FY2025 revenue including a full year of BUKA [S3]; the EV/Sales leg is the 0.848x median of BELI, MCAS, NFCX and WIFI [S0]. (2) Forward roll at the 13.9% cost of equity less the forward dividend gives the base-case Rp468 - the DCF alone would roll to about Rp440, so the EV/Sales weight is worth roughly Rp30 of the Rp485. (3) Scenario probabilities: 50% base (Rp468), 25% bull (Rp625, +5pp revenue growth and +3pp gross margin) and 25% bear (Rp380, mirrored), giving Rp485. The bull weight therefore adds about Rp16. The WACC is 12.8%, INSIDE the 11-13% house band, as is the 12.75% the same asset beta produces on a net-debt basis. What today's price implies: the engine's reverse DCF cannot bracket the price (note "price not bracketed") because at Rp294 the market capitalises the group at an implied operating enterprise value of about Rp5.3tn - market cap less the net cash of Rp22.4tn and the Rp4.4tn investment balance, plus the Rp14.0tn minority - against the DCF's Rp10.9tn, and no revenue-growth path the solver tests closes a gap that size; the price is a statement about the balance-sheet bridge, not an implied permanent revenue collapse [S0, S3].

flags.justification: The weights are 70% DCF and 30% EV/Sales against the 60/40 industry default, and the cross-check is NOT close: it lands 22.4% ABOVE the DCF (Rp472.9 vs Rp386.2) on a 0.848x median EV/Sales built from four IDX internet-platform peers in the data pack - BELI 1.147x, MCAS 0.304x, NFCX 0.549x and WIFI 2.723x [S0]. That divergence is the reason for the weight, not a problem with it: a four-name peer set whose multiples span 0.30x to 2.72x cannot discriminate quality, so it gets less than the 40% default, while the consolidated DCF is the only method that carries the operating cash flow, the tax shield, the net cash bridge and the Rp14.0tn minority claim in one framework [S3, S0]. The 30% weight adds Rp25.9 to the blended value before the roll (Rp412.0 vs the DCF's Rp386.2) and about Rp30 to the target, so it is material but not the sole driver; the report states the divergence plainly rather than calling it confirmation.
